newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Rising output, stocks turn up heat on OPEC.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rising output, stocks turn up heat on OPEC.

text.p: A jump in OPEC oil output and rising industry stocks amplified calls within the cartel for production restraint, but analysts saw little prospect of cuts at next month's meeting in Vienna.

Crude output from the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) hit 27.13 million barrels per day (bpd), up 220,000 bpd from March and surging even further above the group's own ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday.
Equally significant, according to analysts, was the lowest fall in OECD industry oil stocks for any winter since 1990, due to relatively mild weather in the northern hemisphere.
"The absence of a stockdraw in the first quarter of 1997... is seen as a bearish signal for oil markets for the remainder of the year," the Paris-based agency said in its monthly report.

Several OPEC ministers including the group's president, Libya's Abdullah Salem al-Badri, have called this week for the production ceiling to be frozen at the June meeting and for individual members to exercise quota discipline.

Kuwait's oil minister Isa al-Mazeedi, speaking on Thursday at a conference in Iran attended by six other OPEC ministers, said core countries were bearing too much of a burden in propping up world prices.
"Self-discipline is still exercised by a few key members but if this discipline is not maintained I don't dare speculate what prices will do," he said.

A steady increase in exports from Iraq, which returned to the world market in December under a limited United Nations oil-for-food swap, and accelerating output growth at new foreign-company-operated fields makes a reduction in supply extremely unlikely.
"Even when prices fall OPEC won't cut... A prolonged period of oversupply is in prospect," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at UBS Global Research.
World oil prices have slumped by 25 percent, or about $6 a barrel, since the turn of the year, and assuming OPEC fails to reduce output analysts expect further losses as storage tanks fill up.
"Growing supplies have so far been absorbed into stocks but oil in storage will reach maximum desired levels by mid-year," said Pyne.
Company stocks recovered to average historical levels by the end of March and are currently rising by around two million bpd, industry sources said.

"Any boost to oil supplies that threatens to take stocks above the current lower desired level will cause prompt prices to fall sharply," said the Centre for Global Energy Studies in a report released on Friday.

OPEC's Gulf core of Saudi Arabia, UAE and Kuwait, the only members with spare production capacity, oppose proportional cuts based on current output levels, arguing that such a solution would reward quota-busters.

And some analysts and former officials of the 11-member cartel have urged a loosening of OPEC's quota policy, warning that the Middle East's giants are in danger of allowing their massive reserves to lie idle, surrendering even more market share to non-OPEC producers and OPEC colleagues like Venezuela and Nigeria which have attracted foreign investment.
"OPEC is addressing the new issues with oil policies," said Mehdi Varzi, chief oil analyst at finance house Kleinwort Benson.
"There is a real danger the Middle East will not fulfill its potential unless the right fiscal and legislative policies are in place," he said.
